pharm: The R-enantiomer of salbutamol (albuterol); a selective beta2-adrenergic agonist that relaxes airway smooth muscle to relieve and prevent bronchospasm (the FDA label uses the name levalbuterol for the same molecule)
quick: 0.63 mg nebulised three times daily (max 1.25 mg three times daily)
Not applicable - oral inhalation by nebuliser
No adequate human studies; keep asthma controlled, use if benefit outweighs risk
No data on presence in milk; weigh benefits against potential risk
Use caution at high doses (renally excreted; clearance reduced)
Heart rate, blood pressure, serum potassium, frequency of use / asthma control
summary: Levosalbutamol (levalbuterol), the R-enantiomer of salbutamol/albuterol, is a short-acting selective beta2-agonist indicated for treatment or prevention of bronchospasm in patients 6 years and older with reversible obstructive airway disease. It is given by nebuliser; the concentrate must be diluted with sterile normal saline before use. The usual adult/adolescent dose is 0.63 mg three times daily (every 6-8 hours), increased to a maximum of 1.25 mg three times daily if needed, and 0.31 mg three times daily for children 6-11 years (not exceeding 0.63 mg three times daily). Key risks include life-threatening paradoxical bronchospasm, cardiovascular effects (tachycardia, QTc prolongation), hypokalaemia, and the danger that increasing need signals deterioration of asthma requiring anti-inflammatory therapy.
indications: Treatment of bronchospasm in adults, adolescents and children 6 years of age and older with reversible obstructive airway disease
Prevention of bronchospasm in adults, adolescents and children 6 years of age and older with reversible obstructive airway disease

dosage.r: Oral inhalation via nebulisation (dilute concentrate in sterile normal saline)
dosage.d: Starting 0.63 mg; up to 1.25 mg for more severe asthma or inadequate response
dosage.t: Three times a day, every 6 to 8 hours
dosage.n: Monitor patients on the 1.25 mg dose closely for systemic effects; do not exceed the recommended dose

dosage.d: 0.31 mg (routine dosing should not exceed 0.63 mg three times a day)
dosage.n: For doses below 1.25 mg the non-concentrate (pre-diluted 3 mL) formulation must be used

dosage.d: Start at 0.63 mg; may increase as tolerated with monitoring
dosage.n: Increase only with frequent clinical and laboratory monitoring

admin: Dilute the concentrate (1.25 mg/0.5 mL) with sterile normal saline before nebulisation; the pre-diluted 3 mL formulation is used for doses below 1.25 mg
Administer by nebulisation using a standard jet nebuliser (with face mask or mouthpiece) connected to an air compressor
Do not mix with other drugs in the nebuliser - compatibility and safety have not been established
Open the foil pouch just before use; once opened, use the vial immediately and discard the vial if the solution is not colourless
Do not exceed the recommended dose
moa: Levosalbutamol activates beta2-adrenergic receptors on airway smooth muscle, stimulating adenylate cyclase and increasing intracellular cyclic AMP. The rise in cyclic AMP activates protein kinase A, which inhibits myosin phosphorylation and lowers intracellular calcium, producing relaxation of smooth muscle throughout the airways from the trachea to the terminal bronchioles. It acts as a functional antagonist that relaxes the airway irrespective of the constricting stimulus and also inhibits release of mediators from airway mast cells. Although beta2 receptors predominate in bronchial smooth muscle, beta2 receptors are also present in the heart, which can contribute to cardiovascular effects.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to levosalbutamol (levalbuterol) or racemic albuterol (reactions have included urticaria, angioedema, rash, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis and oropharyngeal edema)
relative: Cardiovascular disorders, especially coronary insufficiency, cardiac arrhythmias and hypertension
Convulsive disorders, hyperthyroidism or diabetes mellitus
Patients unusually responsive to sympathomimetic amines
monitor: Heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac symptoms
ECG in patients with cardiovascular disorders (QTc, T-wave, ST changes)
Frequency of use as a marker of asthma deterioration

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Animal studies with levalbuterol showed no teratogenicity, but racemic albuterol was teratogenic in mice (cleft palate) and rabbits (cranioschisis) at doses above the human range. Poorly or moderately controlled asthma increases maternal and fetal risk, so maintain optimal control and use if the benefit justifies the risk. Beta-agonists can interfere with uterine contractility, so use during labour only when benefit clearly outweighs risk; not approved for preterm labour/tocolysis.
lact: There are no data on the presence of levosalbutamol in human milk, its effects on the breastfed child, or on milk production. Consider the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding alongside the mother's clinical need and any potential adverse effect on the infant.
renal: Albuterol is substantially excreted by the kidney and clearance is reduced in renal impairment (a 67% decline in racemic albuterol clearance was seen with creatinine clearance 7-53 mL/min, though half-life was unchanged). Use caution when administering high doses to patients with impaired renal function; the risk of toxic reactions may be greater.
hepatic: The effect of hepatic impairment on the pharmacokinetics of levosalbutamol has not been evaluated.

major: Other short-acting sympathomimetic bronchodilators and adrenergic drugs (including epinephrine) - additive effect; avoid concomitant use and use additional adrenergics with caution to limit cardiovascular effects

Beta-blockers - block the bronchodilator effect and may cause severe bronchospasm; asthmatic patients should not normally receive beta-blockers (use a cardioselective agent cautiously only if no alternative)
MAO inhibitors or tricyclic antidepressants - may potentiate the vascular effects; use with extreme caution during or within 2 weeks of these agents, consider alternative therapy
moderate: Non-potassium-sparing diuretics (loop, thiazide) - ECG changes or hypokalaemia may be acutely worsened; consider monitoring potassium
Digoxin - racemic albuterol decreased serum digoxin levels; consider monitoring digoxin levels
minor: Other asthma/inhaled medications should be used only as directed alongside this drug
interactions.alcohol: Not specifically addressed in the label
interactions.diagnostics: May lower serum potassium and transiently raise blood glucose; consider monitoring potassium and glucose, and ECG in at-risk patients

serious: Life-threatening paradoxical bronchospasm (often with first use of a new vial)
Cardiovascular effects - significant changes in heart rate and blood pressure, ECG changes (T-wave flattening, QTc prolongation, ST depression), arrhythmias
Immediate hypersensitivity reactions (urticaria, angioedema, rash, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis, oropharyngeal edema)
Deterioration of asthma with increasing need for the drug
rare: Changes in blood glucose (may aggravate pre-existing diabetes/ketoacidosis with large doses)
emergency: Cardiac arrest and death have been reported with excessive use of inhaled sympathomimetics
Severe paradoxical bronchospasm - discontinue immediately and treat with alternative therapy

monitoring: Heart rate and blood pressure, especially at higher doses
Serum potassium in patients at risk of hypokalaemia (e.g. with diuretics)
ECG in patients with cardiovascular disorders
Blood glucose in patients with diabetes
Frequency of use and overall asthma control - increasing need signals destabilisation requiring reassessment and possible anti-inflammatory therapy
Renal function when using high doses in renal impairment
counsel: Use exactly as prescribed; do not increase the dose or use it more often than directed without checking with your doctor
If you find you need it more often than usual, it works less well, or your breathing gets worse, seek medical attention promptly - this can mean your asthma is getting worse
This medicine is not a substitute for anti-inflammatory treatment such as inhaled corticosteroids; take your other asthma medicines as directed
Stop the medicine and seek help if your wheezing or breathing suddenly worsens straight after a dose (paradoxical bronchospasm)
Tell your doctor about palpitations, fast heartbeat, chest pain, tremor or nervousness
Dilute the concentrate with sterile normal saline before nebulising and do not mix it with other drugs in the nebuliser
Store in the foil pouch at room temperature, protected from light and heat; open the pouch just before use, use immediately and discard if the solution is not colourless
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or breastfeeding
pk: Rapid bronchodilation within minutes of nebulised dosing (Tmax of R-albuterol about 0.2 hours)
Peak effect within about 1.5 hours; plasma Cmax near 0.2 hours after a single dose
Terminal half-life of R-albuterol about 3.3 hours after a single 1.25 mg dose (about 4 hours after cumulative dosing)
Bronchodilator effect lasts roughly 6 hours (dose every 6-8 hours); slightly longer at the 1.25 mg dose
Store the concentrate in the protective foil pouch at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light and excessive heat; open just before use and use immediately
pearls: Levosalbutamol is the R-enantiomer of salbutamol/albuterol - the FDA label names it levalbuterol; both refer to the same molecule
Paradoxical bronchospasm can be life-threatening and often occurs with the first use of a new vial - discontinue immediately and switch therapy

Increasing need for doses is a marker of deteriorating asthma - reassess the patient and consider adding/optimising anti-inflammatory (corticosteroid) therapy; it is NOT a substitute for corticosteroids
Can cause clinically significant cardiovascular effects (tachycardia, raised BP, QTc prolongation) - use with caution in cardiovascular disease, arrhythmias and hyperthyroidism
May cause transient hypokalaemia (intracellular potassium shift), worsened by non-potassium-sparing diuretics
Do not exceed the recommended dose - fatalities have been linked to excessive use of inhaled sympathomimetics
Beta-blockers can blunt the effect and provoke severe bronchospasm in asthmatics
missed: If a scheduled dose is missed, take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose - do not double up. As a reliever it is used when needed for symptoms; if symptoms are not relieved or doses are needed more frequently than usual, seek medical advice rather than repeatedly increasing the dose.
overdose: Overdose produces exaggerated beta-adrenergic effects: seizures, angina, hypertension or hypotension, tachycardia (rates up to 200 beats/min), arrhythmias, nervousness, headache, tremor, dry mouth, palpitations, nausea, dizziness, fatigue and sleeplessness; hypokalaemia may occur. Cardiac arrest and death can occur with abuse. Management is discontinuation plus supportive symptomatic care; a cardioselective beta-blocker may be considered judiciously, bearing in mind it can provoke bronchospasm. The value of dialysis is not established.
